Nurse -> Riverbend Hospice, this is Tom.
Caller -> Hi, Tom. This is Gideon. I'm calling about my dad, Roland Vickers.
Nurse -> Hi, Gordon. Roland Vickers. And his date of birth?
Caller -> It's Gideon. G I D E O N. May twenty second, nineteen forty.
Nurse -> Sorry about that, Gideon. And I have four oh four, five five five, zero one six four for you?
Caller -> That's right.
Nurse -> What's going on with your dad?
Caller -> His pain is worse. It's his hips, and his lower back. It's been getting worse the last three days.
Nurse -> Okay. How bad is it, zero to ten?
Caller -> He says a five. Maybe a five. It was a three last week.
Nurse -> Okay. What is he taking for pain?
Caller -> The meth a dome. Ten milligrams, three times a day.
Nurse -> And how's that going?
Caller -> It was working. But now it's not enough. So I wanted to ask if I could give him more. Like double the meth a dome.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he sleeping a lot?
Caller -> He sleeps most of the day. More than before.
Nurse -> Okay. And is he throwing up?
Caller -> No. No vomiting.
Nurse -> Okay. Gideon, I can't change the dose over the phone. His pain medicine is one that needs to be adjusted carefully, because it builds up in the body.
Caller -> Okay. But he's hurting.
Nurse -> I understand. I'm going to message our hospice doctor tonight, and ask him to review the pain plan.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> And I'll call you tomorrow morning with the doctor's answer.
Nurse -> When was his last bowel movement?
Caller -> Yesterday morning. It was normal.
Nurse -> Good. And how's his appetite?
Caller -> He's eating a little. A few bites at each meal. Mostly he likes the vanilla pudding.
Nurse -> That's fine. Whatever he enjoys.
Caller -> Yeah. He used to be a big eater. A truck driver, thirty years. He could eat a whole pie.
Nurse -> Ha. Which pie?
Caller -> Pecan. Always pecan.
Nurse -> A man with good taste.
Caller -> My mother used to bake it every Thanksgiving. He still talks about it.
Nurse -> That's a lovely memory. Maybe your sister can make one for him.
Caller -> That's a great idea. I'll ask her. She's the baker.
Nurse -> Even a bite of it might make his day.
Caller -> It would. Thank you for that.
Caller -> One more thing, can I ask? He keeps asking for his old truck keys. He's confused sometimes in the evening. Is that normal?
Nurse -> It can be. Some confusion in the evening is common, especially when someone is sleeping more and not eating much. It's not a surprise, but I'll note it for the doctor.
Caller -> Okay. I just go along with it. I tell him they're in the kitchen drawer.
Nurse -> That's a kind way to handle it. Gentle, no arguing.
Caller -> He gets upset if I correct him. So I don't.
Nurse -> Exactly right. Reassure him, keep the lights on in the evening, and keep things calm.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. That helps, knowing I'm not doing it wrong.
Nurse -> You're doing it right, Gideon.
Nurse -> Does he have a hospice aide coming to help with bathing?
Caller -> Tuesdays and Fridays. She's wonderful. Maria. He calls her his girlfriend.
Nurse -> Ha. Good for him.
Caller -> Tomorrow is Friday, so she'll be here in the morning, right around when you call.
Nurse -> Perfect. I'll call a little after she leaves.
Nurse -> Okay. That's fine. It's the methadone, right? That's what he said.
Caller -> I think so. Yeah. The methadone. That's what's on the bottle. I think. I don't have my glasses on, so I can't really read it.
Nurse -> Okay. Let me see if I can find it in my notes. Hold on.
Caller -> Sure.
Nurse -> I'm not finding it on this screen. I'll have the doctor confirm all the details when he reviews. In the meantime, please give exactly what the label says, and write down each dose and the time on a sheet. And never double up.
Caller -> Okay. Not doubling. I'll write down the times.
Nurse -> For comfort, put pillows under his hips, change his position every two hours, and a warm pack on low, wrapped in a towel.
Caller -> Okay. A warm pack. We have one.
Nurse -> If he gets very sleepy, hard to wake, or his breathing slows down, call me right away. If you can't wake him, nine one one.
Caller -> Okay. I will.
Nurse -> And how are you doing, Gideon? Are you getting any rest?
Caller -> Some. I'm sleeping on the couch next to him. I'm tired, but I'm okay.
Nurse -> Good. Is there anyone who can relieve you for a few hours tomorrow?
Caller -> My sister is coming in the afternoon. She's driving from Savannah.
Nurse -> Good. Take a nap when she gets there.
Caller -> I will. Thank you.
Nurse -> Talk to you tomorrow morning.

Nurse -> Bayview Pediatric Home Care, this is Ingeborg.
Caller -> Hi, Ingeborg. This is Philomena Ashcroft. I'm calling for my daughter. Linnea Ashcroft. I need to order nebulizer supplies.
Nurse -> Hi, Philomena. Okay, let's see what you need. How many neb vials do you have left?
Caller -> I counted six. Six vials. I thought we had more. She's had a cold since Sunday and we've been using them.
Nurse -> Okay. And the mask?
Caller -> Can I ask you to hold for a moment? The kettle is going.
Nurse -> Of course.
Caller -> The mask is cracked. I have one. It's the little elephant one. It cracked at the edge where the strap goes. I've been holding it on her face with my hand.
Nurse -> Don't use a cracked mask. It can leak the medicine. Do you have a spare?
Caller -> No. That's the only one. She doesn't like the other kind. The fish one. She screams at the fish.
Nurse -> Ha. We'll send the elephant. What about the tubing?
Caller -> I appreciate you being patient with me.
Nurse -> Not a problem at all.
Caller -> One set. It looks okay. A little cloudy. I'd like a spare.
Nurse -> Sure. We'll send an extra. How is Linnea doing today?
Caller -> Much better. She had the cough, the wet cough, with the cold. She's still got it, but it's looser. She's eating. She's playing with her dolls.
Nurse -> Has she needed a treatment today?
Caller -> Twice since last night. Once at bedtime and once this morning at six. She was coughing hard at six.
Nurse -> Did it help?
Caller -> Um. Let me think. I'm trying to remember.
Nurse -> Take your time, there's no rush.
Caller -> Yes. She settled right away. She went back to sleep.
Nurse -> Is she wheezing right now? Breathing fast?
Caller -> Wait, say that again? I missed the first part.
Nurse -> Of course. Let me say it slower.
Caller -> No. She's breathing normally. No wheezing. I'm listening. She's humming. She hums when she plays.
Nurse -> Good. Philomena, what's her date of birth?
Caller -> February fourteenth, twenty twenty three. She's three. A Valentine's baby.
Nurse -> Happy early birthday. And a number?
Caller -> Seven one three, five five five, zero one two five.
Nurse -> Got it. I'll order the neb vials, two child masks, and an extra tubing set.
Caller -> Two masks. Yes. Thank you. I'll keep one for the car.
Nurse -> Smart. We'll have them delivered tomorrow.
Caller -> Tomorrow. I'll be home. Is there a time?
Nurse -> The driver will call before. Will you have enough vials for tonight?
Caller -> Six. Yes. If she needs one at bedtime and one in the morning, that's two. Plenty.
Nurse -> And since the mask is cracked, how will you give the treatment tonight?
Caller -> Let me grab my glasses, one second.
Nurse -> Sure, I'll wait.
Caller -> I'll hold the mask on with my hand like I have been. Or use the blow-by. Is that okay?
Nurse -> A cracked mask isn't ideal. Try to hold it as snug as you can. If you can't get a good seal, call me and we'll figure it out.
Caller -> Okay. I'll call.
Nurse -> Let's go over cleaning, too. After every treatment, rinse the cup and the mask with warm soapy water, shake them out, and let them air dry on a clean towel. Don't use a cracked mask.
Caller -> Warm soapy water. Air dry. I do that. Mostly. Sometimes I just rinse and leave it on the counter.
Nurse -> Soap and air dry is better. Germs can grow in a wet cup.
Caller -> Okay. I'll be better about it.
Nurse -> Call us if her breathing gets fast or hard, if a treatment doesn't help, or if she has a fever of one hundred two or higher. If her lips turn blue, call nine one one.
Caller -> Fast breathing. Treatment doesn't help. A hundred two. Blue lips, nine one one. Okay.
Nurse -> Great. Does she have a thermometer?
Caller -> Yes. The ear one. We use it a lot.
Nurse -> Good. Anything else you need?
Caller -> No. I think that's it. Oh, can I ask? She keeps taking the mask off and trying to put it on her doll. Is that a problem?
Nurse -> Ha. Not at all. It can help her get used to it. Let her put it on the doll first.
Caller -> Sorry, I'm writing this down as we go.
Nurse -> Good idea. I'll pause.
Caller -> That's what the other nurse said. She calls it the doll doctor game.
Nurse -> Ha. Let her be the doctor.
Caller -> She's very serious about it. She has a stethoscope. She listens to my chest and tells me I have a cold.
Nurse -> Ha. A good diagnosis.
Caller -> She's not wrong. I do have a cold.
Nurse -> Take care of yourself too.
Caller -> Okay. I'm back. What was the question?
Nurse -> I'll repeat it, no trouble.
Caller -> I will. Thanks, Ingeborg.
Nurse -> Bye, Philomena.
Caller -> Bye.

Caller -> Oh god. Okay. Okay. Hold on. Greg! Greg, come here! Call nine one one! Dad fell! Hit his head!
Nurse -> Is Greg calling?
Caller -> He's on it. He's calling. Okay. I'm still here.
Nurse -> Good. Press a clean towel firmly on the cut. Don't lift it to peek. If it soaks through, put another one on top, and keep pressing.
Caller -> Pressing. Firm. Okay. It's coming through. I'm putting another one on.
Nurse -> That's right. Keep pressing. Is he on any blood thinners?
Caller -> Yes. Warfarin. He takes it every evening. Five milligrams. He took it last night.

Caller -> Warfarin. I'll tell them. Greg! Tell the dispatcher he's on warfarin!

Caller -> He says his head hurts. He says it's a bad one. A headache, behind his eye. It wasn't there before he fell.
Nurse -> Has he vomited? Did he pass out, even for a second?
Caller -> No. No vomiting. He didn't pass out. I heard the thump and I ran in and he was awake. He was sitting up already.
Nurse -> Okay. Keep him still. Don't let him stand or walk around. Keep him lying down, or sitting against the wall if that's more comfortable. Don't move his neck.
Caller -> Wait, say that again? I missed the first part.
Nurse -> Of course. Let me say it slower.
Caller -> He's against the wall. He wants to get up. I'm telling him no. Dad, stay. Stay put.
Nurse -> That's right. Give him nothing by mouth. No water, no food, no pills.
Caller -> No pills. He has his evening pills on the counter. Do I give him anything?
Nurse -> No. None of them. Especially not the warfarin. Don't give him any of his medicines until the doctors say so.
Caller -> No pills. Okay. I'm putting them away. Not yet. Hold on, I'm pressing. I can't. Okay. Greg's got the pills.
Nurse -> Good. Tell me when the dispatcher says they're on the way.
Caller -> Greg says they're sending an ambulance. They said ten minutes. Ten minutes.
Nurse -> Perfect. Stay with him. What's his date of birth, Annalise? For the paramedics.
Caller -> December fifteenth, nineteen thirty eight.
Nurse -> And the best number to reach you?
Caller -> Two oh six, five five five, zero one nine eight. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Got it. I'm going to page the on-call clinician right now so they know what's happening.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. Please.
Nurse -> Is the bleeding slowing at all?
Caller -> I don't know. Hold on. I can't look. If I lift it, it'll start again. The towel's heavy.
Nurse -> Don't lift. Just keep the pressure steady.
Caller -> Sorry, the dog is barking. Hold on.
Nurse -> Ha, no worries.
Caller -> Okay. I'm leaning on it. He's wincing.
Nurse -> I know. It hurts, but it's important. Talk to him. Keep him awake. Ask him his name, where he lives.
Caller -> Dad, what's your name? Sylvester. Where do you live? Dad? He says Cedar Street. That's right. And he said the year. He said nineteen... no, he said the wrong year.
Nurse -> What year did he say?
Caller -> He said twenty ten. It's twenty twenty six.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell the paramedics that, too. He's confused about the date.
Caller -> Okay. I'm back. What was the question?
Nurse -> I'll repeat it, no trouble.
Caller -> I will. I'll tell them everything.
Nurse -> Does he have any allergies or other health conditions you can tell them? Heart problems? Diabetes?
Caller -> He has atrial fibrillation. That's why the warfarin. And high blood pressure. No diabetes. No allergies I know of.
Nurse -> Good. Tell them all that. Is there a list of his medicines?
Caller -> On the fridge. A printed list. Greg is grabbing it for them.
Nurse -> Perfect. Annalise, are you hurt? Did you fall?
Caller -> Okay. Sorry about that. Go on.
Nurse -> Alright, thank you.
Caller -> No. I'm fine. I'm just scared. My hands are shaking. I'm covered in his blood.
Nurse -> That's okay. You're doing great. Wash up after they take over, and wear gloves if you have them.
Caller -> I'll wash. I don't have gloves.
Nurse -> It's fine. Keep going.
Caller -> I hear something outside. Is that the sirens? Hold on. Greg, is that them?
Nurse -> Take your time. I'm here.
Caller -> Sorry, I'm writing this down as we go.
Nurse -> Good idea. I'll pause.
Caller -> Yes, yes, they're pulling up. Greg's going to the door. Okay. Here they come.
Nurse -> Good. Tell the paramedics the warfarin and the wrong date. They'll take it from here.
Caller -> I will. Thank you. Thank you, Valentina.
Nurse -> Go ahead. We'll follow up with the family.
Caller -> Okay. Bye.

Nurse -> Okay. So three earlier, and six now.

Caller -> The aide said she ate about a quarter of her lunch. But the dietary sheet says she ate half. So I don't know which is right.
Nurse -> Okay. So between a quarter and half.
Caller -> Yes. I'm sorry that I can't be more precise.

Nurse -> Any falls?

Caller -> Perfect.

Caller -> Yesterday, I think. I'd have to check the flow sheet. I can look when we hang up.
